subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 17! In this unit you will learn how shapes and points move around a grid. Every day the world around you is full of movement. A door swings open, a bicycle wheel spins, your face appears flipped in a mirror, and the tiles on a masjid floor repeat their pattern across the whole room. All of these are examples of transformations – the mathematical study of how objects slide, turn and flip while keeping their true shape.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Read and write coordinates as ordered pairs (x, y) and plot points accurately.
Identify the four quadrants and work with positive and negative coordinates.
Perform and describe translations using movement in units and vectors.
Perform and describe reflections across the x-axis, y-axis and the lines y = x and y = -x.
Perform and describe rotations of 90°, 180° and 270° about the origin, clockwise and anticlockwise.
Use coordinate rules to calculate the image of a point under any transformation.
Recognise line symmetry and rotational symmetry in shapes and patterns.
Apply and describe combinations of transformations and understand that order can matter.
Predict and describe the image of a shape reflected in a mirror line that is not parallel or perpendicular to the axes, by measuring perpendicular distance to the line.
Predict and describe the image of a shape rotated 90° about one of its own vertices, rather than about the origin.

concepts.title: The Coordinate Grid and Four Quadrants
concepts.explanation:
Before we can move shapes, we need a precise way to say where they are. The coordinate grid does exactly this. It is built from two number lines that cross at right angles. The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis. They meet at a special point called the origin, which has coordinates (0, 0).

The two axes divide the whole grid into four regions called quadrants. We number them with Roman numerals, starting at the top right and going anticlockwise:

Quadrant I (top right): both coordinates positive, like (4, 3), form (+, +).

Quadrant II (top left): x negative, y positive, like (-4, 3), form (–, +).

Quadrant III (bottom left): both negative, like (-4, -3), form (–, –).

Quadrant IV (bottom right): x positive, y negative, like (4, -3), form (+, –).

Understanding negative coordinates is one of the big new skills of Year 6. In earlier years you may have used only the top-right quadrant, where everything is positive. Now the grid stretches in all four directions, just like a real map has places east and west, north and south of a central town. If the origin is the well at the centre of a village, then (3, 2) might be Yusuf's house to the north-east, while (-3, -2) is Halima's house to the south-west. The sign of each number tells you the direction; the size of each number tells you the distance.
concepts.example: When you read a point that already sits on the grid, work backwards: first count how far left or right it is from the y-axis to get the x-coordinate, then count how far up or down it is from the x-axis to get the y-coordinate. Points that sit exactly on an axis have a zero in one coordinate. For example (5, 0) sits on the x-axis, and (0, -4) sits on the y-axis. The origin (0, 0) is the only point that belongs to both axes at once.

concepts.title: Plotting and Reading Points
concepts.explanation:
Plotting a point means marking its exact position on the grid. Follow these steps every time and you will never go wrong. To plot the point (4, 3):

Move 4 units right along the x-axis, because the x-coordinate is 4.

From there, move 3 units up, parallel to the y-axis, because the y-coordinate is 3.

Mark the point clearly with a small cross or dot.

Now try a point with negative numbers, such as (-2, -3). Start at the origin, move 2 units left (because x is -2), then 3 units down (because y is -3). You end up in Quadrant III. Notice how the signs guide the direction at every step. Always deal with the x-coordinate first and the y-coordinate second – mixing them up is the single most common error, and it lands your point in the wrong place entirely.

Reading points is the reverse skill. Suppose a point is marked on the grid. Drop a straight line down to the x-axis to read the x-coordinate, then slide across to the y-axis to read the y-coordinate. Write them in brackets, x first. Coordinates are used for real problems too. We can find the distance between two points that share a coordinate. Points (4, 2) and (4, 6) lie on the same vertical line because their x-coordinates match, so the distance between them is simply |6 - 2| = 4 units. Likewise (3, 4) and (8, 4) share a y-coordinate, so their distance is |8 - 3| = 5 units.
concepts.example: Coordinates power an astonishing amount of modern life. GPS satellites pinpoint your phone using coordinates. Every pixel on a screen has a coordinate address. Architects place walls using coordinate plans, and video games track every character and object by its coordinates. When Ibrahim plays a football game on a phone, the ball's position is stored as a pair of numbers updated many times each second. Mastering the grid connects you directly to this technology.

concepts.title: Translations (Sliding)
concepts.explanation:
A translation is the simplest transformation. It slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. Imagine pushing a book across a table: it moves, but it does not turn and it does not flip. A translation is exactly like this smooth slide.

Translations have important properties. The shape keeps its size – nothing grows or shrinks. It keeps its orientation – it does not rotate, so it always faces the same way. Every side length and every angle stays exactly as it was. Because the original and its image are identical in every measurement, we say they are congruent. Only the position changes.

We describe a translation using a vector, written as a pair of numbers that tells us how far to move horizontally and vertically. The vector (4, -1) means “4 units right and 1 unit down”. A positive first number means right, negative means left; a positive second number means up, negative means down. To find the image of a point, simply add the vector to the coordinates. Translate (2, 3) by the vector (4, -1): new x is 2 + 4 = 6, new y is 3 + (-1) = 2, so the image is (6, 2).

When we translate a whole shape, we apply the same rule to every vertex. Take a triangle with corners at (1, 1), (3, 1) and (2, 4). Translate it 5 right and 2 down, which is the vector (5, -2). Add (5, -2) to each corner: (1, 1) becomes (6, -1), (3, 1) becomes (8, -1), and (2, 4) becomes (7, 2). We label the image with prime notation: if the original is triangle ABC, the image is triangle A′B′C′, read “A prime, B prime, C prime”. Each original vertex matches its own primed image.
concepts.example: Two translations done one after another combine into a single translation. If Sahra slides a counter 3 right and 2 up, then slides it 1 left and 4 up, the total movement is (3 - 1) right and (2 + 4) up, which is 2 right and 6 up, or the vector (2, 6). To reverse a translation, you use the inverse vector – travel the same distance the opposite way. The inverse of (4, -1) is (-4, 1), which slides the shape neatly back where it started.

concepts.title: Reflections (Flipping)
concepts.explanation: A reflection creates a mirror image of a shape across a line called the line of reflection or mirror line. Think of holding a shape up to a mirror: the image is the same distance behind the glass as the object is in front, and it appears flipped. Every point of the shape has a matching point on the other side, and the mirror line sits exactly halfway between them. Like translations, reflections keep the shape congruent — the size and all the measurements stay the same. What changes is the orientation: the shape… So far these mirror lines have been horizontal, vertical, or the diagonals y = x and y = -x, which line up neatly with the grid. A mirror line can also be any other straight line, drawn at any angle, that is not parallel or perpendicular to the axes. To reflect a shape in a mirror line like this, measure the perpendicular (right-angle) distance from each point of the shape to the mirror line, then mark the reflected point the same perpendicular distance on the opposite side of the line. Every reflected point stays exactly as far from the mirror line as the original point, just on the other side, and the line joining an original point to its reflected image always crosses the mirror line at a right angle.

concepts.title: Rotations (Turning)
concepts.explanation: A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point called the centre of rotation. Every point of the shape sweeps along a circular path around this centre, and every point turns through the same angle. Picture the hands of a clock sweeping around, or a wheel spinning on its axle — both are rotations about a central point. To describe a rotation fully you must state three things: the centre it turns around (often the origin), the angle it turns through (usually 90°, 180° or 270°), and the direction — clockwise or… Rotations do not always happen around the origin of the grid. A shape can also be rotated about one of its own vertices (corners) — in this case, that vertex acts as the centre of rotation and stays completely fixed in place, while every other point of the shape sweeps around it through the given angle, such as 90°. To find the image of a shape rotated 90° about one of its own vertices, keep that vertex exactly where it is, then rotate each of the other vertices around it by measuring the same angle and the same distance from the fixed vertex, in the chosen direction (clockwise or anticlockwise).

concepts.title: Describing and Identifying Transformations
concepts.explanation:
Being able to perform a transformation is only half the skill. You must also be able to look at a shape and its image and describe the transformation that connects them. Good descriptions use precise mathematical language, and each type of transformation needs its own set of details.

To describe a translation, give the vector or say how many units left/right and up/down, for example “a translation by the vector (5, -2)”.

To describe a reflection, name the mirror line, for example “a reflection in the y-axis” or “a reflection in the line y = x”.

To describe a rotation, give the centre, angle and direction, for example “a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin”.

How do you decide which transformation has happened? Look for clues. If the image is the same size and the same way up, it is a translation – measure how far it has slid. If the image is flipped or reversed, like a mirror image, it is a reflection – find the line that sits halfway between object and image. If the image has been turned, so it faces a new direction but is not a mirror image, it is a rotation – find the point that stays the same distance from matching corners.
concepts.example: A neat way to check a reflection is to fold: if folding the paper along your chosen line makes the object land exactly on its image, you have found the correct mirror line. To find a centre of rotation, join two matching points to their images and see where the shape appears to pivot. With practice, you will recognise each transformation at a glance, the way Khadija can tell whether a pattern on a dress was made by sliding, flipping or turning the same motif.

methods.title: How to plot a point
methods.example: In which quadrant does the point (-3, 5) lie?
steps: Start at the origin (0, 0).
Move left or right by the x-coordinate.
Move up or down by the y-coordinate.
Mark the point with a small cross.

methods.title: How to describe a transformation
methods.example: A shape is reflected so that (2, 3) maps to (-2, 3) and (4, 1) maps to (-4, 1). Describe the transformation.
steps: Translation: give the vector or the units left/right and up/down.
Reflection: name the mirror line (x-axis, y-axis, y = x, and so on).
Rotation: give the centre, the angle, and the direction.
Check: the image is always congruent to the original.

methods.title: How to rotate with tracing paper
methods.example: Rotate the point (2, 5) by 180° about the origin using tracing paper.
steps: Trace the shape and mark the centre of rotation.
Hold a pencil point firmly on the centre.
Turn the paper the required angle and direction.
Mark where the shape now sits — that is the image.

methods.title: Reflect across the y-axis
methods.example: Reflect the point (5, 3) across the y-axis.
steps: The rule for the y-axis is (a, b) → (-a, b).
Only the x-coordinate changes sign, so (5, 3) becomes (-5, 3).
The point flipped from the right side of the grid to the left, staying at the same height.

methods.title: Reflect across y = x
methods.example: Reflect the point (-2, 3) across the line y = x.
steps: The rule for y = x is (a, b) → (b, a) — swap the coordinates.
So (-2, 3) becomes (3, -2).
Swapping is all you do for this special diagonal mirror line.

methods.title: Rotate 90° clockwise
methods.example: Rotate the point (3, 2) by 90° clockwise about the origin.
steps: The rule is (a, b) → (b, -a).
So the new x is the old y (2), and the new y is the negative of the old x (-3).
The image is (2, -3).
You can check this with tracing paper: mark the point, pin the origin, and turn a quarter turn clockwise.

workedExamples.title: Name the quadrant
workedExamples.prompt: In which quadrant does the point (-3, 5) lie?
workedExamples.solution: The x-coordinate is negative and the y-coordinate is positive, giving the form (–, +). That is Quadrant II, the top-left region. Always read the signs: minus x means left, plus y means up.

workedExamples.title: Translate a point
workedExamples.prompt: Translate the point (-1, 4) by the vector (2, -5).
workedExamples.solution: Add the vector to the coordinates. New x = -1 + 2 = 1. New y = 4 + (-5) = -1. The image is (1, -1). The point has slid 2 right and 5 down.

workedExamples.title: Translate a triangle
workedExamples.prompt: A triangle has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1) and (2, 4). Translate it 5 right and 2 down.
workedExamples.solution: The vector is (5, -2). Add it to each vertex: (1, 1) → (6, -1); (3, 1) → (8, -1); (2, 4) → (7, 2). So triangle A′B′C′ has vertices (6, -1), (8, -1) and (7, 2). Every corner moved the same way, so the triangle stays congruent.

workedExamples.title: Reflect across the y-axis
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point (5, 3) across the y-axis.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for the y-axis is (a, b) → (-a, b). Only the x-coordinate changes sign, so (5, 3) becomes (-5, 3). The point flipped from the right side of the grid to the left, staying at the same height.

workedExamples.title: Reflect across y = x
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point (-2, 3) across the line y = x.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for y = x is (a, b) → (b, a) — swap the coordinates. So (-2, 3) becomes (3, -2). Swapping is all you do for this special diagonal mirror line.

workedExamples.title: Rotate 90° clockwise
workedExamples.prompt: Rotate the point (3, 2) by 90° clockwise about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: The rule is (a, b) → (b, -a). So the new x is the old y (2), and the new y is the negative of the old x (-3). The image is (2, -3). You can check this with tracing paper: mark the point, pin the origin, and turn a quarter turn clockwise.

workedExamples.title: Rotate 180°
workedExamples.prompt: Rotate the point (-3, 1) by 180° about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: The rule is (a, b) → (-a, -b). Both signs flip, so (-3, 1) becomes (3, -1). A half turn always sends a point to the opposite side of the origin.

workedExamples.title: Combine two transformations
workedExamples.prompt: Apply to the point (1, 4): first reflect across the x-axis, then rotate 90° clockwise about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1, reflect across the x-axis using (a, b) → (a, -b): (1, 4) becomes (1, -4). Step 2, rotate 90° clockwise using (a, b) → (b, -a): (1, -4) becomes (-4, -1). The final image is (-4, -1). Do the steps strictly in order.

workedExamples.title: Describe a transformation
workedExamples.prompt: A shape is reflected so that (2, 3) maps to (-2, 3) and (4, 1) maps to (-4, 1). Describe the transformation.
workedExamples.solution: In each pair the y-coordinate stays the same and the x-coordinate changes sign. That is the rule for the y-axis. So the transformation is a reflection in the y-axis (the line x = 0).

workedExamples.title: Rotate 90° anticlockwise
workedExamples.prompt: Rotate (4, 1) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for a 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin is (a, b) → (-b, a). So the new x is the negative of the old y (-1), and the new y is the old x (4). The image is (-1, 4).

workedExamples.title: Combine two translations
workedExamples.prompt: A shape is translated by (4, 2), then by (-1, 3). Write the single equivalent vector.
workedExamples.solution: Add the two vectors together: x = 4 + (-1) = 3, y = 2 + 3 = 5. The single equivalent vector is (3, 5). Two translations performed one after another always combine into one overall translation.

workedExamples.title: Reflect (0, 4) across the line x = 3
workedExamples.solution: For a reflection in the vertical line x = 3, find the distance from the point to the line and go the same distance on the other side: the distance from x = 0 to x = 3 is 3, so the image x-coordinate is 3 + 3 = 6. The y-coordinate stays the same. The image is (6, 4).

activities.title: Make Your Own Four-Quadrant Grid
steps: Draw a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis crossing at the centre of your page.
Number both axes from -5 to 5, marking the origin as (0, 0).
Ask a family member (or your AI tutor) to call out coordinate pairs and plot each one - or pick your own pairs to plot if no one is available.
For each point, say aloud which quadrant it is in, or whether it sits on an axis.
Keep this grid – you can use it for every activity in this unit.

activities.title: The Sliding Tile (Translation)
activities.materials: a small object such as a bottle cap, and your grid.
steps: Place the cap on a starting point, for example (1, 1).
Roll two dice (or pick two numbers) to make a translation vector, such as (3, 2).
Slide the cap the right amount and read off its new coordinates.
Write the translation as ‘started at ___, vector ___, finished at ___’.
Notice the cap never turns or flips – that is what makes it a translation.

activities.title: Mirror Magic (Reflection)
activities.materials: a small mirror, squared paper, a pencil.
steps: Draw a simple shape, such as an L, on one side of a line (try the y-axis).
Write the coordinates of two matching points and see how the rule (a, b) → (-a, b) works.
Try the same shape with the mirror on the x-axis and on the diagonal line y = x.

activities.title: Tracing-Paper Turns (Rotation)
activities.materials: tracing paper (or thin paper), a pencil, your grid.
steps: Draw a small flag shape on the grid and trace it onto the tracing paper.
Press your pencil point firmly on the origin to hold it as the centre of rotation.
Turn the tracing paper a quarter turn (90°) clockwise and mark the new position.
Repeat for 180° and 270°, and compare your marks with the coordinate rules.

activities.title: Symmetry Hunt (Investigation)
steps: Walk around your home, the masjid, or the market and look for symmetry.
Record objects with line symmetry (leaves, doors, patterns) and draw their mirror lines.
Record objects with rotational symmetry (wheels, flowers, fans) and estimate their order.
Sort your finds into a table and share the most surprising one with your teacher.

activities.title: Design a Tessellation (Family or Group Task)
steps: Cut out one simple shape, such as a square or triangle, as your tile.
Cover a sheet of paper by sliding (translating) the tile again and again with no gaps.
Now try flipping and turning the tile to make a more interesting repeating pattern.
Colour your design like the tiles in a mosque and name the transformations you used.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand transformations best? Which transformation – sliding, flipping or turning – felt trickiest? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Coordinates Rule
rules.text: Write points as (x, y): x first (left/right), y second (up/down). Along the corridor, then up the stairs. The origin is (0, 0).

rules.title: Quadrants Rule
rules.text: Quadrant I: (+, +). Quadrant II: (–, +). Quadrant III: (–, –). Quadrant IV: (+, –).

rules.title: Translation Rule
rules.text: Add the vector to each coordinate. Vector (4, -1) means 4 right and 1 down.

rules.title: Reflection Rule
rules.text: Reflect in the x-axis: (a, b) → (a, -b). Reflect in the y-axis: (a, b) → (-a, b). Reflect in the line y = x: (a, b) → (b, a). Reflect in the line y = -x: (a, b) → (-b, -a).

rules.title: Rotation Rule
rules.text: For rotations about the origin: 90° clockwise (a, b) → (b, -a); 90° anticlockwise (a, b) → (-b, a); 180° (a, b) → (-a, -b). A 270° clockwise turn gives the same image as a 90° anticlockwise turn.

rules.title: Symmetry and Combining Transformations Rule
rules.text: A shape has line symmetry if a mirror line splits it into two matching halves, and rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a turn of less than 360°. When combining transformations, always apply them in the order given - doing them in a different order can give a different final image.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Apply to (2, 3): first translate by (4, 1), then reflect across the y-axis. Give each stage and the final point.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1) Translate by (4, 1): (2, 3) becomes (6, 4). 2) Reflect (6, 4) across the y-axis: it becomes (-6, 4). The final point is (-6, 4).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Show, using the point (3, 2), that reflecting across the x-axis and then the y-axis is the same as a single 180° rotation about the origin.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Reflect in the x-axis: (3, 2) becomes (3, -2). Then reflect in the y-axis: (3, -2) becomes (-3, -2). A single 180° rotation about the origin sends (3, 2) to (-3, -2) directly, using the rule (a, b) → (-a, -b). Both methods give the same image, (-3, -2), so the two reflections combined are equivalent to a 180° rotation.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A triangle (2, 1), (4, 1), (3, 3) is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin. Find the image vertices.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Using the rule (a, b) → (b, -a) for a 90° clockwise rotation about the origin: (2, 1) → (1, -2); (4, 1) → (1, -4); (3, 3) → (3, -3). The image triangle has vertices (1, -2), (1, -4) and (3, -3).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Point (3, 1) rotates to (-1, 3). State the angle and direction of the rotation about the origin.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Using the rule (a, b) → (-b, a) for a 90° anticlockwise turn: (3, 1) → (-1, 3), which matches. So the rotation is 90° anticlockwise about the origin.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Does order matter? Test (3, 2): Method A translate by (1, 1) then reflect in y-axis; Method B reflect in y-axis then translate by (1, 1). Compare the results.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Method A: translate (3, 2) by (1, 1) to get (4, 3), then reflect in the y-axis to get (-4, 3). Method B: reflect (3, 2) in the y-axis to get (-3, 2), then translate by (1, 1) to get (-2, 3). The two methods give different results, (-4, 3) and (-2, 3), so order does matter when combining transformations.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Describing and Identifying Transformations.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Being able to perform a transformation is only half the skill. You must also be able to look at a shape and its image and describe the transformation that connects them. Good descriptions use precise mathematical language, and each type of transformation needs its own set of details. To describe a translation, give the vector or say how many units left/right and up/down, for example “a translation by the vector (5, -2)”.

rounds.prompt: Rotate the point (4, -3) by 180° about the origin. What is the image?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: A 180° rotation about the origin uses the rule (a, b) → (-a, -b), so (4, -3) becomes (-4, 3).

rounds.prompt: A point (2, 5) is first translated by (3, -1), then reflected in the x-axis. What is the final image?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Translate first: (2, 5) becomes (5, 4). Then reflect in the x-axis: (5, 4) becomes (5, -4).

games.title: Unit Champion: Translation
games.description: Practise translation through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Quadrant” mean?
choices: One of the four regions of the grid
A slide described by a vector
A flip across a mirror line
A turn about a centre
rounds.answer: One of the four regions of the grid
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 17 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Quadrant means One of the four regions of the grid.

rounds.prompt: Translate the point (2, -3) by the vector (5, 4). What is the image?
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: Add the vector to the point: 2 + 5 = 7 and -3 + 4 = 1, so the image is (7, 1).

rounds.prompt: What is the image of (5, 2) after a reflection in the line y = x?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Reflecting in the line y = x swaps the coordinates, so (5, 2) becomes (2, 5).

rounds.prompt: A shape is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin, so (2, 3) maps to (3, -2). Using the same rule, what does (4, -1) map to?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: The rule for a 90° clockwise rotation about the origin is (a, b) → (b, -a). Applying it to (4, -1) gives (-1, -4).

selfAssessment: I can read and write coordinates as ordered pairs (x, y) and plot points accurately.
I can identify the four quadrants and work with positive and negative coordinates.
I can perform and describe translations using movement in units and vectors.
I can perform and describe reflections across the x-axis, y-axis and the lines y = x and y = -x.
I can perform and describe rotations of 90°, 180° and 270° about the origin, clockwise and anticlockwise.
I can use coordinate rules to calculate the image of a point under any transformation.
I can recognise line symmetry and rotational symmetry in shapes and patterns.
I can apply and describe combinations of transformations and understand that order can matter.
